original_answer:
The paper uses a rich set of textual features: theme-based features (modeling emotions, stance, and other changes per theme), NLI-style writing features (bag of stopwords, POS tags, syntactic dependency relations), and profiling features.

The approach is "mainly based on textual features which utilize thematic information, and profiling features to identify the accounts from their way of writing tweets" [2]. Textual features are modeled independently for each theme to capture emotional, stance, and other changes in users' tweets [1]. Theme-based features include emotions, computed with the NRC emotions lexicon (~14K words labeled with Plutchik's eight emotions), motivated by IRA efforts to seed discord (e.g., fear-spreading behavior) [9]. For detecting writing-style patterns, they use NLI features consisting of a bag of stopwords, part-of-speech tags (POS), and syntactic dependency relations (DEPREL) [6]. These are combined with surface text features, and the extracted themes boosted performance when coupled with them [8].

Therefore, in this paper, we propose a text-based approach to detect the online trolls such as those that were discovered during the US 2016 presidential elections. Our approach is mainly based on textual features which uti- lize thematic information, and proﬁling features to identify the accounts from their way of writing tweets. We deduced the thematic information in a unsupervised way and we show that coupling them with the textual features enhanced the performance of the proposed model.

Thus, we use state-of-the-art NLI features to detect this unique pattern [8,23,14]; the feature set consists of bag of stopwords, Part- of-speech tags (POS), and syntactic dependency relations (DEPREL). Our experiments showed that the extracted themes boosted the per- formance of the proposed model when coupled with other surface text features. In addition, we proposed NLI features to identify IRA trolls from their writing style, which showed to be very eﬀective. Finally, for a better understanding we analyzed the IRA accounts from emotional and linguistic perspectives. Through the manually checking of IRA accounts, we noticed that frequently irony was employed.

For that, we use the NRC emotions lexicon [25] that contains ∼14K words labeled using the eight Plutchik’s emotions.
